 Judgment

This appeal is filed by the appellant under Section 29 of Protection of women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (in short 'PWDV Act') challenging the order dated 26.12.2023 passed on IA No.2 by the learned MMTC-VI, Bengaluru in Crl.Misc.No.50/2023 and directed to pay maintenance of Rs.10,000/- to the petitioners No.1 and 3 from the date of petition till the disposal of the petition.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 2. By the aforesaid order dated 26.12.2023, the trial court was pleased to partly allow IA No.2 and the respondent therein directed to pay maintenance of Rs.10,000/- p.m. to the petitioners No.1 and 3 from the date Crl.A.No.29/2024 of petition till disposal of the petition.
3. The respondent is appellant in this appeal.
The petitioners No.1 and 3 are the respondent No.1 and parties are referred to their ranks as ranks in this appeal for the sake of convenience.
4. The grounds urged in the appeal, is briefly stated as follows.
The appellant married the respondent No.1 on 27.05.1999 and their marriage is love marriage.
Out of the marriage, the respondents No.2 and 3 are born.
The appellant is employed in National Scheduled Caste Financial Developmental Corporation, and it is a Central Government Undertaking / PSU.

entities.text: National Scheduled Caste Financial Developmental Corporation
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: The appellant presently working as Assistant General Manager at Bengaluru Unit.
He would retire in the month of February 2027.
He purchased the shared house by obtaining the loan from the bank.
The outstanding loan is amounting to Rs.37 lakhs, he has to pay monthly EMI of Rs.50,000/-.
His mother is aged 92 years and he has to look after her.
She is retired Government teacher.
The appellant is taking care of the respondents and Crl.A.No.29/2024 providing all facilities to them.
When he expressed his willingness to sell the flat shared house, then the respondent No.1 started to object for the same.
The respondent No.1 insisted for transfer of apartment to her name for which the appellant did not agreed.
The respondent No.1 started quarrelling with the appellant almost everyday and started non-co-operation at home.
She stopped cooking food for family members and started harassing the aged mother of the appellant.
The respondent No.2 also joined the respondent No.1.
They have filed this Crl.Misc.No.50/2023 before the MMTC-VI alleging domestic violence.
The respondent filed the objection to the main petition and produced the documents.
The respondent No.1 moved IA No.2 for maintenance and also filed IA No.I to restrain the appellant from alienating the apartment.
The learned Magistrate granted exparte order dated 19.04.2023 which came to be challenged by the appellant by preferring appeal in Crl. Appeal No.732/2023.

sentences.text: the same came to be dismissed for the reasons that the order being exparte, the appellant can approach the Magistrate for disposal of IA No.I Crl.A.No.29/2024 on merits.
IA No.2 filed by the respondent No.1 for interim maintenance partly allowed.
Challenging the order the appellant has preferred the appeal.

It is not in dispute that the appellant and the respondents are in the same shared household and the appellant is providing each and every items of the provisions including milk, groceries, vegetable, school and college fees of respondents No.2 and 3 including cooking gas.
The respondents are not entitled for interim maintenance.

In addition to all, the appellant is paying electricity bill and water bill, monthly maintenance of the apartment, traveling bus charges for respondent No.3 to attend the school daily, tour and travel charges, TV cable charges etc.
The home-take salary, after deduction of EMI of the appellant is Rs.80,000/- only.

Out of this amount,
the appellant spending entire amount for taking care of the respondents and his aged mother and to meet other financial expenses.
The respondent No.1 has become totally hostile towards the appellant and aged mother.
She is not cooking food for them.
Even though mediation was held, it was failed due to adamant stand of the respondents.
The Crl.A.No.29/2024 respondent No.1 has no intention of matrimonial ties and renounced world of matrimonial relation with the appellant without any justifiable and legal reasons.
Consequently, the appellant has been suffering financially and all sorts of inconvenience.

The appellant has filed the M.C. No.4658/2023 before the II Addl. Family Judge,
Bengaluru seeking for restoration of conjugal rights.
In that petition, the respondent No.1 has sought divorce.
The appellant is suffering cruelty in the hands of the respondents No.1 and 2.

The respondent No.1 is in the habit of going out of the house during evening times and attend late night parties till midnight and come home in the midnight, as if the appellant is nobody to question her and her outside program and activities.
At the instigation of sister of the respondent No.1 who is residing in Singapore, the respondent No.1 cut the relationship with the appellant.
On account of these the appellant suffering mental torture and loneliness.
The respondents No.1 and 2 are seeing the appellant as if he is their enemy at home, though the appellant and the respondents are living in the shared household.
It would Crl.A.No.29/2024 contend that the learned Magistrate has presumed that selling or alienating the apartment without permission of the family members is a kind of domestic violence.
This imagination of the learned Magistrate is totally arbitrary and capricious and not acceptable under law.
5. In this case, there is no material whatsoever in support of the domestic violence by the appellant.
The learned Magistrate presumed that only evidence provided by the respondent No.1 as sufficient.
The respondent No.1 except production of the photo of broken latch not produced any other materials to demonstrate that the appellant has given ill treatment.
The respondent No.1 falsely cooked up this latch broking story.
It was broken by the respondent No.1 herself.
In the absence of any evidence of domestic violence the learned Magistrate erroneously passed an order to pay maintenance amount.

Hence, on these among other grounds, the appellant prays to set aside the order passed by the learned Magistrate on IA No.2.
Crl.A.No.29/2024 6.
The respondents entered appearance by engaging their counsel.
In this appeal, the learned counsel for the appellant as well as learned counsel for the respondents produced documents.

sentences.text: Heard arguments of the learned counsel for the appellant and the learned counsel for the respondents and perused the records.

8. The following points would arise for my consideration:-
Point No.1: Whether the order of the trial court dated 26.12.2023 on IA No.2 regarding order to pay maintenance suffers from any illegality, irregularity and as such calls for interference by this court in the appeal?
Point No.2: What order?
9. My findings to the above points are as below:-
 Point No.1
In the NEGATIVE.
Point No.2: As per the final order, for the  following  REASONS 10.
POINT NO.1:

The present respondent No.1 has filed petition u/s.12 of PWDV Act against the present appellant before the learned MMTC-VI, Bengaluru seeking protection Crl.A.No.29/2024 order u/S.18 of PWDV Act, residence order u/S.19 of PWDV Act, Monetary relief u/S.20 of PWDV Act,
compensation / damages u/S.22 of PWDV Act and also prayed for relief u/S.21 of PWDV Act.

The learned Magistrate by allowing interlocutory application filed by the respondent No.1 passed protection order, maintenance order and also passed order restraining the present appellant for alienating the shared household.
Since the appellant has filed separate appeal challenging the order passed on IA No. 1 and 3 with regarding restraining him from selling the property.

I would not discuss about the same in this appeal and the same is discussed in Crl. Appeal No.1570/2024.
11.
In the present appeal, the appellant would contend that there is no domestic violence in order to grant any such interim maintenance in favour of the respondents.
Hence, first and foremost point to be considered in this appeal whether there is domestic violence or not.
It is important to refer the definition clause of PWDV Act.
The definition of domestic violence is defined u/S.3 of PWDV Act which reads Crl.A.No.29/2024 as follows.
"3. Definition of domestic violence.--For the purposes of this Act, any act, omission or commission or conduct of the respondent shall constitute domestic violence in case it--

sentences.text: (a) harms or injures or endangers the health, safety, life, limb or well-being, whether mental or physical, of the aggrieved person or tends to do so and includes causing physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse and economic abuse; or (b) harasses, harms, injures or endangers the aggrieved person with a view to coerce her or any other person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any dowry or other property or valuable security; or (c) has the effect of threatening the aggrieved person or any person related to her by any conduct mentioned in clause (a) or clause (b); or (d) otherwise injures or causes harm, whether physical or mental, to the aggrieved person.

Explanation I.--For the purposes of this section,--
(i) "physical abuse" means any act or conduct which is of such a nature as to cause bodily pain, harm, or danger to life, limb, or health or impair the health or development of the aggrieved person and includes assault, criminal intimidation and criminal force;

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, on plain reading of S.3 of PWDV Act, different kinds of domestic violence, such as physical abuse, mental abuse, economic abuse, verbal and emotional abuse are stated.
The disposal of household effects and alienation of any assets whether movable and immovable is also comes Crl.A.No.29/2024 within the definition of economic abuse.
While addressing the arguments, it came to know to this court that during the pendency of the proceedings, the appellant has already sold one site standing in his name.
The appellant as well as respondent No.1 have filed their assets and liability affidavit before the learned Magistrate.
On perusal of the affidavit of the assets and liabilities filed by the present respondent No.1 it would go to show that she is not having any income of her own.
The respondent No.3 is minor and school going boy.
It is submitted that the respondent No.2 now completed Law graduation.
The learned Magistrate has not awarded any maintenance in favour of the respondent No.2.

On the other hand, on perusal of the assets and liabilities statement of the appellant it would go to show that he is working as Assistant General Manager in the National Scheduled Caste and Financial Developmental Corporation, which is a Central Government Undertaking / PSU.

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: According to the appellant his home take salary is Rs.80,000/- after deduction of EMI of Rs.50,000/-, which itself indicates that the appellant was having salary of Crl.A.No.29/2024 Rs.1,30,000/- as on date of filing of his assets and liabilities in the year 2023-24.
The appellant in his assets and liabilities declared that he owning two sites one in his name and another site is in the name of respondent No.1.
He is owner of the apartment wherein the appellant and the respondents are residing as a shared household.

13. On perusal of the copy of the petition filed u/S/12 of PWDV Act, the respondents have made allegations against the appellant regarding domestic violence i.e. cruelty, both mental and physical meted out by the appellant on them.
The learned Magistrate rightly held that when consideration application for interim relief only requirement is to make out prima facie case.
The court need not go into deep on merits of the case.
On perusal of the petition filed u/S.12 of PWDV Act.
there is clear allegations made against the appellant that he harassed the respondent both mentally and financially.
According to the appellant himself he intends to sell the shared household which indicates that he want to evict them from the shared household.

Protection u/S.3(iv)
Crl.A.No.29/2024 (b) of PWDV Act very clear that economic abuse includes any alienation of any assets whether movable or immovable are affect rights of the victim to reside in the shared house.
The learned Magistrate has rightly come to the conclusion that there is domestic violence which comes within the definition of S.3 of PWDV Act.

sentences.text: No doubt, the respondents have not denied regarding appellant spending amount towards purchase of certain home necessity items.
In the present case, the respondents have also produced documents such as grocery bills, to show that the respondents also purchased some groceries.

The learned counsel for the respondent produced document such as copy of sale deed dated 30.09.2023,
encumbrance certificate of the property which would go to show that, during the pendency of the proceedings the appellant sold site standing in his name.
The learned counsel of the respondents produced photographs to show that the original suit is pending with respect to site standing in the name of respondent No.1.
The respondents also produced copy of Crl.A.No.29/2024 petition in Crl.Misc.No.90/2023 which would go to show that the mother of the appellant filed petition u/S/PWDV Act against the respondents.
The respondents also produced copy of objection filed in M.C.No.4658/2023, copy of First Information Report to show that the respondent No.2 filed criminal case against the appellant.
The respondents also produced photographs to show the appellant possessing Range Rover car.
They have also produced photograph to show that the appellant has stored grocery items separately in the shared house.

On the other hand, the appellant has also produced the documents such as grocery purchased bills, food bills, food items, medical bills, Online shopping bills, gas purchase bill, school bus fare bill, vegetable and fruits bills, clothes purchase bills, food consumption at hotel, household sanitary bills for the period from August 2023 to January 2024.
The appellant has also produced copies of documents to show that the respondent No.1 has also filed complaint to his higher authorities.

On perusal of the documents produced by the appellant as well as respondents one thing is very clear that there are several Crl.A.No.29/2024 criminal cases and civil case are filed between the parties.
Now the relationship between the parties are in strained condition.
15. Admittedly, the appellant is having salary more than Rs.1,30,000/- p.m. as on the date of impugned order.
When considering maintenance application we have to consider all the necessities of the aggrieved person.

Provision u/S.20 (1)
(d) of PWDV Act is very clear that maintenance for the aggrieved person as well as her children, if any, including an order under or in addition to an order of maintenance u/S.125 of CrPC or any other last for time being in force.
Sub-Clause(2) is very clear that relief granted under this section shall be adequate, fair and reasonable and consistent with the standard of living to which aggrieved person is accustomed.

No doubt, on perusal of the records, it would go to show that the appellant used to purchase grocery items, food and medicine clothes and spending other expenses such as school fees of the respondents No.2 and 3 traveling expenses.

But as the appellant and the Crl.A.No.29/2024 respondent No.1 are not in good terms, the respondent No.1 being custodian of her minor son, the respondent No.3, she cannot always beg to the appellant for her daily needs.
Even if the respondent No.1 is home maker her contribution in taking care of her sons respondents No.2 and 3 cannot be undermined.

The learned Magistrate by taking into account the needs and expenses of the respondents No.1 and 3, and earning capacity of the appellant directed the appellant to pay amount of Rs.10,000/- p.m. to the respondents No.1 and 3.
When compared to the salary of the appellant it is only meager amount.
Nobody can lead standard of living without spending atleast Rs.200/ per day for maintenance.

When compared to the standard of living of the appellant and the respondents and considering earing capacity of the Vijaykumar R Salkute vs Mrunal V Salkute on 17 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/83528603/
7 appellant the maintenance of Rs.10,000/- p.m. ordered by the learned Magistrate is very meager one.

sentences.text: Admittedly, the respondent No.1 has to look after her minor son respondent No.3.

Even though the appellant would contend that the respondent No.1 not providing food to him and his mother, but he has not disputed that the respondent No.1 cooking Crl.A.No.29/2024 food to the respondents No.2 and 3.
There is no income of respondent No.1 of her own.
She and her minor son respondent No.3 entirely dependent on the income of the appellant.
The court cannot always monitor affairs of the appellant and the respondents.
What is going on inside the house of the appellant and the respondents known to them only we can decide the case based on the pleadings and documents and evidence.
On perusal of the petition filed u/S.12 of PWDV Act present respondents have made clear allegations against the appellant that he has committed domestic violence.
Even in the assets and liabilities statement, the appellant has stated that he has donated gold of R.2 lakhs to the temple.

For what reason he has donated is irrelevant, but the fact remains that he has donated such huge amount of gold in favour of the temple itself shows the financial capacity of the appellant.
16.

By considering the necessity of the respondents No.1 and 3 and earning capacity of the appellant,
the trial court rightly directed to pay the amount of Rs.10,000/- p.m. to the Crl.A.No.29/2024 present respondents No.1 and 3.
According to the appellant his mother is aged about 94 years who is retired Government teacher from Maharashtra.
Under such circumstances, she would have been getting pension.
On the other hand, the entire records would go to show that the respondents are not having income of their own.
Even there is document to shows that the respondent is taking care of household expenses, but still the respondents No.1 and 3 are require the maintenance amount for their livelihood
. The order passed by the learned Magistrate not warrants for interference at the hands of this appellate court.
Rate of maintenance order fixed by the learned Magistrate is not illegal, it is based on the correct reasoning.
Hence, by considering the submission of both sides and perusal of the record, this court is of the opinion that there is no error in passing the maintenance order by the learned Magistrate.
Hence, I answer Point No.1 in the Negative.

17. POINT NO.2:- In view of my findings on Point No.1, I proceed to pass the following Crl.A.No.29/2024 ORDER Appeal filed by the appellant U/s.29 of Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is hereby DISMISSED.
